content: Respiratory distress affects approximately 7% of newborns, necessitating respiratory support (RS) that can be delivered invasively via an endotracheal (ET) tube or non-invasively through a nasal interface. Invasive ventilation is associated with an increased risk of lung injury and chronic lung disease (CLD). Non-invasive strategies, with or without minimally invasive surfactant administration, may help reduce the need for mechanical ventilation and the associated risk of lung damage in newborns with respiratory distress. The objective of this study was to assess the benefits and potential harms of nasal high-frequency ventilation (nHFV) compared to invasive ventilation via an ET tube or other non-invasive ventilation methods in preterm and term infants with or at risk of respiratory distress. The analysis included randomized controlled trials (RCTs), cluster-RCTs, or quasi-RCTs comparing nHFV to other forms of respiratory support. A total of 33 studies were identified, involving 5068 preterm and 46 term infants, primarily conducted in lowto middle-income settings. The findings are summarized as follows: 1. nHFV vs. Invasive Ventilation for Initial Respiratory Support: There is significant uncertainty regarding whether nHFV reduces mortality before hospital discharge (RR 0.67, 95% CI 0.20 to 2.18; 1 study, 80 infants) or the incidence of CLD (RR 0.38, 95% CI 0.09 to 1.59; 2 studies, 180 infants). The evidence is of very low certainty. Outcomes such as ET intubation, death or CLD, severe intraventricular hemorrhage (IVH), and neurodevelopmental disability (ND) were not reported. 2. nHFV vs. Nasal Continuous Positive Airway Pressure (nCPAP) for Initial Respiratory Support: There is very low certainty regarding whether nHFV reduces mortality before hospital discharge (RR 1.00, 95% CI 0.41 to 2.41; 4 studies, 531 infants). nHFV may reduce the need for ET intubation (RR 0.52, 95% CI 0.33 to 0.82; 5 studies, 571 infants). There may be little or no difference in the incidence of CLD (RR 1.35, 95% CI 0.80 to 2.27; 4 studies, 481 infants), death or CLD (RR 2.50, 95% CI 0.52 to 12.01; 1 study, 68 participants), or severe IVH (RR 1.17, 95% CI 0.36 to 3.78; 4 studies, 531 infants). The evidence is of low certainty. ND was not reported. 3. nHFV vs. Nasal Intermittent Positive-Pressure Ventilation (nIPPV) for Initial Respiratory Support: nHFV may result in little to no difference in mortality before hospital discharge (RR 1.86, 95% CI 0.90 to 3.83; 2 studies, 84 infants; low certainty). nHFV may have little or no effect on reducing ET intubation (RR 1.33, 95% CI 0.76 to 2.34; 5 studies, 228 infants; low certainty). There may be a reduction in the incidence of CLD (RR 0.63, 95% CI 0.42 to 0.95; 5 studies, 307 infants; low certainty). A single study (36 infants) reported no events of severe IVH. Death or CLD and ND were not reported. 4. nHFV vs. High-Flow Nasal Cannula (HFNC) for Initial Respiratory Support: There is very low certainty regarding whether nHFV reduces ET intubation (RR 2.94, 95% CI 0.65 to 13.27; 1 study, 37 infants) or the incidence of CLD (RR 1.18, 95% CI 0.46 to 2.98; 1 study, 37 participants). No mortality events before hospital discharge or severe IVH were reported. Other outcomes, including death, CLD, and ND, were not reported. 5. nHFV vs. nCPAP Following Planned Extubation: nHFV probably results in little or no difference in mortality before hospital discharge (RR 0.92, 95% CI 0.52 to 1.64; 6 studies, 1472 infants; moderate certainty). nHFV may reduce the risk of ET reintubation (RR 0.42, 95% CI 0.35 to 0.51; 11 studies, 1897 infants) and the incidence of CLD (RR 0.78, 95% CI 0.67 to 0.91; 10 studies, 1829 infants). Both findings are of low certainty. nHFV probably has little or no effect on the combined outcome of death or CLD (RR 0.90, 95% CI 0.77 to 1.06; 2 studies, 966 infants) or severe IVH (RR 0.80, 95% CI 0.57 to 1.13; 3 studies, 1117 infants). Both findings are of moderate certainty. There is very low certainty regarding whether nHFV reduces ND (RR 0.92, 95% CI 0.37 to 2.29; 1 study, 74 infants). 6. nHFV vs. nIPPV Following Planned Extubation: nHFV may have little or no effect on mortality before hospital discharge (RR 1.83, 95% CI 0.70 to 4.79; 2 studies, 984 infants; low certainty). nHFV probably reduces the risk of ET reintubation (RR 0.69, 95% CI 0.54 to 0.89; 6 studies, 1364 infants). There is probably little or no effect on the incidence of CLD (RR 0.88, 95% CI 0.75 to 1.04; 4 studies, 1236 infants), the combined outcome of death or CLD (RR 0.92, 95% CI 0.79 to 1.08; 3 studies, 1070 infants), or severe IVH (RR 0.78, 95% CI 0.55 to 1.10; 4 studies, 1162 infants). These findings are of moderate certainty. One study reported that there might be no difference in ND (RR 0.88, 95% CI 0.35 to 2.16; 1 study, 72 infants; low certainty). 7. nHFV vs. nIPPV Following Failure of Initial Non-Invasive Respiratory Support: nHFV may have little or no effect on mortality before hospital discharge (RR 1.44, 95% CI 0.10 to 21.33), ET intubation (RR 1.23, 95% CI 0.51 to 2.98), the incidence of CLD (RR 1.01, 95% CI 0.70 to 1.47), or severe IVH (RR 0.47, 95% CI 0.02 to 10.87). These findings are based on a single study with 39 participants and are of low or very low certainty. Other outcomes, including death, CLD, and ND, were not reported. In conclusion, for initial respiratory support, there is significant uncertainty regarding the impact of nHFV on clinical outcomes compared to invasive respiratory therapy. However, nHFV may reduce the need for intubation when compared to nCPAP. Following planned extubation, nHFV may reduce the risk of reintubation compared to nCPAP and nIPPV and may reduce the risk of CLD when compared to nCPAP. After the failure of initial non-invasive respiratory support, nHFV may result in little to no difference in intubation rates compared to nIPPV. Further large-scale trials, particularly in high-income settings, are needed to clarify the role of nHFV in initial respiratory support and following the failure of other non-invasive methods. Additionally, optimal nHFV settings require further investigation.
